To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) a small number of insolation curves, selected from a very large number of potential curves, can account for the majority of the variance in four different proxy records, and that (2) this result is consistent with the Milankovich paradigm, in which high-latitude insolation variations are the primary forcing mechanism.
the insolation curves that explain Quaternary proxy data most effectively are those with the following properties: high latitudes, non-noon, and similar absolute latitudes to the proxy records.

(1) insolation curves from specific latitudes and/or times of day can explain the proxy curves better than does the Milankovicht paradigm; and (2) insolation curves that are similar in latitude and/or time of day to the location of the proxy record tend to be selected by the model.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the problem of finding the best fit of a linear combination of insolation records to a paleoclimatic proxy.
developing a methodology for objectively identifying which insolation curves, individually or in combinations, best explain paleoclimatic proxy records.
the problem of determining which combination of insolation time-series best explains a paleoclimatic proxy record.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the insolation curves we found to explain the proxy data are not the “true” ones, but that they are plausible explanations for the paleoclimatic changes.
a large fraction of the variability in the proxy records is explained by a weighted combination of insolations, but the exact nature of that combination varies with the proxy record.
insolation, as a forcing function for paleoclimatic change, is not limited to the Milankovitic paradigm.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
insolation is a significant factor, but that other factors are also significant.
the Milankovicht paradigm, as currently conceived, is not a sufficient explanation of Quaternary climate, and that a more comprehensive approach is required.
the insolation curves that explain the proxy data most effectively are those that are most similar in latitude and season to the region and season where the proxy data are collected.
The main takeaway from our work is that
linear programming is a promising new tool for paleoclimatic analysis, and it can be applied to other types of data as well.
the inductive linear programming approach provides a powerful tool to identify plausible insolation curves that can explain a paleoclimatic dataset.
a large number of plausible explanations for paleoclimatic variation exist.
